title: Parallel plans: critical paths, slack and what a delay changes

concepts.name: earliest-finish
outcomes: Translate finish-to-start arrows into maximum predecessor finish, not a sum of concurrent work.
Compute earliest starts/finishes and common project finish under explicit unlimited parallelism.

concepts.name: latest-times-and-slack
outcomes: Work backward from the earliest project finish and calculate total slack.
Distinguish an individual allowed delay from independently spendable slack along several sequential jobs.

concepts.name: critical-branches
outcomes: Identify all zero-slack jobs and tight critical arrows, including tied branches.
Explain why shortening one tied branch alone need not shorten project finish; separate zero-duration milestones from disconnected slack.

concepts.name: scope-and-changes
outcomes: Predict when a duration change exhausts slack and changes the critical set.
Refuse cyclic timing under the declared DAG model, and state that calendar, staffing, probabilistic duration and real-project guarantees are outside scope.

assumptions.edge: X -> Y means X must finish before Y starts
assumptions.timingDomain: DAG; cycles produce no timing result

changes: Draft 3 -> 4 makes both branches critical while finish stays 7.
Summing all four durations gives 10 and is not the earliest parallel finish.
Shorten Draft alone from 4 to 3: finish remains 7.
Shorten both Draft and Review from 4 to 3: finish becomes 6.

handComputedExamples.note: Start -> Done is a true prerequisite but not tight; the disconnected zero-duration Note has slack 5. An all-zero DAG instead has finish and slack zero for every job.
A delay of 3 before First consumes the branch margin; adding another 3-unit wait before Second would delay Join. The two reported slacks cannot simply be summed as independent budget.
The model refuses a whole-plan timing table; it still distinguishes cycle members, blocked descendants and the independent ready job.
